summary: A proposed Telnet protocol from the committee, circulated before the Atlantic City meeting. Telnet lets a user at one computer log in to another across the network as if directly attached. It was meant to give early implementers a common basis and was not final. RFC 139 gives background and RFC 158 revised it.

eli5.summary: Telnet is like a long invisible cable to a far computer. This draft shows how to build that cable so many different computers can use it.

subtitle: The committee's first full proposal for Telnet: a shared virtual terminal so any user terminal can drive any host.

tldr.problem: Hosts on the network have different terminals and conventions, and each host should not have to track the quirks of every other host.
tldr.mechanism: Telnet defines a Network Virtual Terminal that uses full ASCII in 8-bit bytes, with a few control codes (high bit set) for things like break, echo and data type.
tldr.outcome: It was circulated before the Atlantic City meetings so early implementers shared one basis. It was a proposal, and RFC 139 updates it.

facts.label: NVT code
facts.value: 7-bit ASCII in 8-bit bytes, high bit zero

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 139 as an update to this proposal and gives its status as unknown. The RFC describes itself as a proposed document, not a final standard.

sections.title: Purpose and Status of the Proposal
sections.content:
This is an April 1971 request for comment from the Telnet committee, distributed ahead of the Atlantic City meetings. It also gives selected installations planning early implementations a common basis. The committee felt the protocol was adequate for initial implementation, and the chairman folded in a few recent suggestions that were not fully cleared with all members.

Telnet is a third-level protocol that makes a terminal or process at a using site look, to a serving site, logically equivalent to a terminal directly connected there. It tries to minimize what each host must know about the others.
sections.eli5: A group of people wrote a first plan and shared it early so everyone building it would start from the same page.

sections.title: Protocol Levels and Roles
sections.content:
The RFC defines three levels. Level 1 is the host-to-IMP protocol. Level 2 is the host-to-host protocol performed by the NCPs. Level 3 is where the NCP communicates internally in its own host: the Telnet process runs there at using sites, and the Telnet server runs there at serving sites.

Telnet uses the established Network Control Program and the Initial Connection Protocol (ICP). The using site hosts the Telnet process; the serving site is the host the user's keyboard input is directed into. The user is the person or process driving the Telnet process.
sections.eli5: The network is built in layers, like floors of a building. Telnet lives on the top floor and uses the floors below to carry its messages.

sections.title: The Network Virtual Terminal
sections.content:
Telnet provides a Network Virtual Terminal (NVT). Its code is full ASCII: the seven-bit code is sent in eight-bit bytes with the high-order bit zero. The using site must give users a way to produce all 128 ASCII codes plus a set of special Telnet control signals.

The serving site specifies how NVT code maps to the codes a local terminal would produce, ideally one for one for ASCII graphics and controls. The ASCII character ESC is the escape signal showing that the next character or characters have special meaning, and its meaning is defined by the serving site. The end of a line is carriage return followed by line feed. The protocol assumes the serving site initially provides no echo.
sections.eli5: Everyone agrees to talk through an imaginary standard keyboard and screen. Each computer only has to translate between its own terminal and that imaginary one.

sections.title: Control Codes
sections.content:
Each Telnet control signal sent over the connection is one eight-bit code with the high-order bit set to one. The listed codes cover a data type signal (X'A0', meaning seven-bit ASCII), an order to send an INS and insert X'80' in the data stream, Break or Attention (X'81'), Reverse Break (X'82', from the serving system), I Echo (X'83'), You Echo (X'84'), a not-implemented notice (X'87') and return to control mode (X'88'). X'85' and X'86' are reserved.

A one-byte DATA TYPE signal is sent first on a connection; if the first byte has its high bit zero, seven-bit ASCII NVT is assumed. A site that receives a DATA TYPE signal responds with a double X'88' if the new type is acceptable.

Two local signals need no network code: transmit all data so far, and suppress the end-of-line transmission while sending all other data. Data goes to the NCP as convenient, but at least at end of line, end-of-line suppression and transmit signals.
sections.eli5: Special bytes with a big first bit act like traffic signs in the stream: stop, I will repeat what you type, or I did not understand that sign.

items.label: DATA TYPE (ASCII)
items.desc: Both sites; data will use seven-bit ASCII NVT conventions.

items.label: Send INS
items.desc: Using site orders its NCP to send an INS and insert X'80' in the data stream.

items.label: Not implemented
items.desc: This site has not implemented the following control code.

items.label: Return to control mode
items.desc: Next byte will be a control signal, possibly a new DATA TYPE.
